text.p: A bout of profit-taking and a drooping dollar/mark hauled sterling/mark off the fresh 30-month highs it made in early trade, dealers said.
Sterling powered to 2.5260 marks in early Europe but had pulled back to 2.5110/20 by 1454 GMT.
"There's bound to be a bit of profit-taking. It's had a good one-way run without much of a correction so sooner or later it's going to stall," said Bank of Boston forex dealer Peter Wood.
News that the U.S. trade deficit ballooned by a hefty 10.1 percent in September knocked dollar/mark and by proxy the pound, overshadowing an earlier slew of buoyant UK data.
UK M4 money supply leaped 10.3 percent in October, while retail sales jumped four percent in the three months to October versus the same period a year ago, the largest rise since September 1994.

The 0.4 percent month-on-month retail sales increase matched forecasts, but analysts noted that the headline figure masked strong growth in textile, clothing and footwear sales, where prices had already risen strongly in recent months.
"The upward pressure on interest rates is still there, and therefore the upward pressure on the currency is still there," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

Sterling remained more robust against the dollar, although it slipped from the fresh four-year high of $1.6820 touched in morning Europe. It traded at $1.6765/75 at 1512 GMT compared to $1.6755/65 here late yesterday.
On a trade-weighted basis it stood at 92.1, down from an intrasession high of 92.4 -- its strongest since September 1992 -- and the previous close of 92.3.

The market spotlight is now on the next monetary meeting between Bank of England governor Eddie George and Chancellor Kenneth Clarke on December 11, with speculation intensifying that interest rates will be hiked then.
Rates were raised by a quarter-point on October 30.

"Despite sterling strength and the rate rise on October 30, there is a continued feeling that policy is too loose and ought to be tightened, and there's a feeling the Chancellor may well do it," said Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch.
"To that extent it ought to be a small positive for sterling," he added.

The immediate focus, before the monetary meeting, is the UK budget on November 26. Monday's data showing a 4.393 billion stg October public debt repayment helped calm market fears that Clarke would deliver a fiscally-imprudent package.
Members of parliament's Treasury Select Committee back economists' predictions, telling Reuters they expect a prudent budget and a penny cut off income tax.

"What the (October 30) interest rate rise shows is that his budget is going to be a cautious budget. It's not going to be an electioneering budget," said Matthew Carrington, the Conservative chairman of the panel.
Thursday sees the release of final third-quarter UK GDP and revised second-quarter balance of payments data.
